assessment: Dopamine loss in Parkinson's disease results in impaired movement initiation and execution, but the precise relationship between dopamine activity and the decision to move is poorly understood. Here, the authors imaged mesostriatal dopamine signals as head-fixed mice decided when, after a cue, to retrieve water from a spout. Surprisingly, ramps in dopamine activity predicted, even on single trials, the timing of licks. Fast ramps preceded early retrievals; slow ones preceded late ones. Optogenetic activation or suppression of dopamine activity accelerated or delayed lick initiation, respectively. Together, these findings reveal strong links between ramps in dopamine activity and the timing of self-initiated movement.
